title: Ζεὺς καὶ πίθος ἀγαθῶν
titleEn: Zeus and the Jar of Good Things
part: Zeus and the Jar of Good Things (Chambry 123 · Perry 312)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 123 (= Perry 312). Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ζεὺς ἐν πίθῳ τὰ ἀγαθὰ πάντα συγκλείσας ἀφῆκε παρὰ ἀνθρώπῳ τινί.
sentences.tr: Zeus en pithōi ta agatha panta synkleisas aphēke para anthrōpōi tini.
sentences.l: Zeus, having shut all the good things up together in a jar, left it with a certain man.
sentences.n: A πίθος is the great earthenware store-jar, tall as a man and often sunk into the floor, not a small pot. It is the same vessel as in the more famous story, where what is shut in are the evils and what stays behind in the jar is hope. παρά with the dative is 'at the side of', of the person in whose keeping a thing is left.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ λίχνος ἄνθρωπος εἰδέναι θέλων τί ἐστιν ἐν αὐτῷ, τὸ πῶμα ἐκίνησε· πάντα δὲ ἐπετάσθησαν πρὸς τοὺς θεούς.
sentences.tr: Ho de lichnos anthrōpos eidenai thelōn ti estin en autōi, to pōma ekinēse· panta de epetasthēsan pros tous theous.
sentences.l: But the greedy man, wishing to know what was in it, shifted the lid; and they all flew away to the gods.
sentences.n: λίχνος is the appetite word — greedy after dainties, and so, of the mind, itching to taste what is not one's own. ἐπετάσθησαν is aorist passive in form but active in sense, as often with πέτομαι: they took wing of themselves. πρὸς τοὺς θεούς says where the good things belong; men had them only on deposit.

sentences.t: Ὅτι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις ἐλπὶς μόνη σύνεστι τῶν πεφευγότων ἀγαθῶν ἐγγυωμένη δώσειν.
sentences.tr: Hoti tois anthrōpois elpis monē synesti tōn pepheugotōn agathōn engyōmenē dōsein.
sentences.l: That hope alone keeps company with men, going surety that it will give of the good things that have fled.
sentences.i: The story shows that hope alone keeps company with men, going surety that it will give of the good things that have fled.
sentences.n: Ὅτι can only subordinate — it cannot open a sentence any more than English 'that' can. The introducing verb is unexpressed in the Greek and is supplied in the idiomatic line. σύνειμι with the dative is to be in someone's company: hope is the one that stayed behind. ἐγγυάομαι is the legal word for standing surety, and it takes the future infinitive δώσειν of what is guaranteed; the genitive τῶν πεφευγότων ἀγαθῶν reads most naturally as partitive with that infinitive — hope pledges some part of what has gone, which is as much as hope can pledge. πεφευγότων is perfect: they have fled and are still away.
